questions.question: In an LWE sample b = A·s + e (mod q), what is the purpose of the error term e?
options: It hides the exact linear relation so recovering s becomes hard
It ensures A is always invertible over Z_q by construction
It lets you compute s by taking b mod e for each coordinate
It turns modular arithmetic into real-valued arithmetic
questions.explanation: Without error, the system is just linear equations; adding small error is what creates hardness while keeping structure.

questions.question: If the error term e were exactly zero and you had enough equations, what is the most direct way to recover s?
options: Solve the linear system for s over Z_q using linear algebra
Run a discrete logarithm algorithm on the entries of A
Use a hash preimage attack on b to recover s directly
Use a timing side-channel attack on the decryption routine
questions.explanation: With e = 0, b = A·s (mod q) is a standard linear system that can be solved (when it has full rank / enough rows).

questions.question: For parameters n (secret dimension) and m (number of equations), what are the shapes of A and b in LWE?
options: A is m×n and b is length m, both modulo q
A is n×m and b is length n, both modulo q
A is n×n and b is length n, both over the reals
A is m×m and b is length m, both over the integers
questions.explanation: LWE publishes m noisy equations in n unknowns: A has m rows and n columns, and b has one entry per equation.

questions.question: In the toy Regev-style encryption in this lesson, why add μ·(q/2) to v (mod q)?
options: To encode the bit as a value far from 0 so it survives small noise
To make the ciphertext always have the same v for any message bit
To guarantee the secret s becomes uniformly random mod q
To ensure the matrix A has orthogonal columns over Z_q
questions.explanation: Placing 0 and q/2 as separated targets lets decryption decide which one x is closer to even after adding small noise.

questions.question: During decryption we compute x = v - u^T·s (mod q). In the ideal (small-noise) case, x should be near what?
options: Near 0 when μ=0, and near q/2 when μ=1 ideally
Near a uniformly random value in {0,1,...,q-1} always
Near the determinant of A when μ=0 or μ=1 always
Near the length of the secret vector s for any μ
questions.explanation: Subtracting u^T·s cancels the A·s structure, leaving the message offset plus a relatively small noise term.

questions.question: Attack intuition: why does brute forcing a ternary secret s ∈ {-1,0,1}^n stop working as n grows?
options: Because the search space size grows as 3^n and explodes quickly
Because Gaussian sampling becomes undefined when n is large
Because modular addition stops being associative when n is large
Because the ciphertext no longer contains u and v when n is large
questions.explanation: Even with a tiny alphabet, the number of candidates grows exponentially in n, making exhaustive search infeasible.

questions.question: What does a center-lift function do in an LWE implementation?
options: Map a residue mod q into a small signed representative like [-q/2, q/2]
Convert a real Gaussian into an exact integer distribution over Z
Turn a matrix multiplication into a vector addition modulo q
Make the public matrix A uniformly random without an RNG every time
questions.explanation: Center-lifting helps interpret residues as small signed errors, which is useful for debugging and toy attacks.

questions.question: What is a common failure mode if q is too small compared to the total noise in encryption and key generation?
options: Decryption fails because values wrap around the decision boundary mod q
Key generation fails because SHA-256 outputs fewer than q bits
Encryption fails because A stops being a matrix when q is small
Decryption succeeds for any noise level as long as q is prime
questions.explanation: If noise is large relative to q, modular wrap-around can move x closer to the wrong target (0 vs q/2).
